r: The applied work spans two registers: conceptual knowledge of microorganisms, ingredients, and preservation chemistry, and the hands-on laboratory practice of actually fermenting beer, wine, cider, mead, and vegetable ferments under strict sanitation, then evaluating outcomes through sensory analysis and building an original product. Task-exposure research places manual and physical work, along with judging a ferment by smell and taste, well outside AI's automatable range, even as a model can draft recipes or explain fermentation pathways. The graded competence is embodied: developing calibrated observational judgment at the bench and a trained palate. These map to O*NET activities for handling objects, monitoring processes, and inspecting materials. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on fermentation technique is not eroded; automation touches the writing and planning shell, not the physical making the course is built around.

By 2031, generative tools will fluently propose recipes, model fermentation kinetics, and draft the historical and cultural framing the course requires, offloading more of the preparatory and documentary work. That augments the learner rather than substituting for the wet-lab core: a student still must sanitize equipment, pitch and manage live cultures, and diagnose a stalled or contaminated ferment in real time. Verification burden is real because a mishandled ferment carries food-safety consequences whose failure modes are not obvious until tasting, exactly the condition that keeps embodied competence necessary. Diffusion of AI into hands-on food-production instruction lags capability, as adoption data broadly shows. Across a catalog cycle the laboratory requirement holds. The rating stays Low; the tools reshape analysis and presentation, not the physical fermentation practice the course exists to build.

Over a decade, automated and instrumented fermentation systems will grow more capable in industrial settings, and simulation could absorb more pre-lab planning and predictive analysis. Even so, the specific competence this introductory course develops, a student personally acquiring sanitation discipline, sensory evaluation, and physical fermentation technique across beer, wine, and vegetable ferments, is not a task AI performs on the learner's behalf; embodiment is the point. The most plausible ten-year shift is in how much descriptive and analytical work migrates to AI around a still-human making-and-tasting core, not in whether the hands-on competence is needed. The honest uncertainty concerns the balance of simulated versus physical lab time; the rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and by perceptual judgment that observed-usage data shows sits far from where AI is actually deployed.
BVG 1910.d: This course explores the science, history, and practice of fermentation through both lecture and hands-on laboratory activities. Students will learn the roles of microorganisms, ingredients, and equipment in producing a wide variety of fermented foods and beverages, including beer, wine, cider, mead, and vegetable-based ferments. Emphasis is placed on proper sanitation, recipe development, and the cultural and nutritional significance of fermentation as a method of preservation, flavor enhancement, and food safety. Throughout the course, students will apply fermentation methods in the lab, evaluate outcomes, and ultimately develop and present their own fermented product, supported by historical or cultural context, process documentation, and sensory analysis.

r: The applied work is beverage-operations management: equipping, staffing, and marketing a bar, restaurant, hotel, or event program; procuring and selecting quality beverages for sustainable operations; and reviewing the world's major commercial beverages to inform purchasing. These map to O*NET activities for developing strategies, coordinating others, and influencing customers, precisely the managerial and marketing tasks observed-usage data shows as a prominent and growing share of AI use, and that task-exposure research associates positively with exposure through their writing- and planning-heavy character. The course does include practical appraisal of beverage preparation and service, which is embodied and somewhat protective. But the dominant graded competence is management and procurement knowledge work. At 24 months adoption is still uneven and the human still directs decisions, so the instrumental need is only partly eroded; the rating sits at Medium.

By 2031, AI planning, demand forecasting, procurement optimization, menu and marketing drafting, and staffing tools will be broadly deployed in hospitality operations, and enterprise deployments already skew heavily toward automation of exactly these back-office tasks. The instrumental case for learning to plan, cost, market, and manage a beverage program erodes materially as models generate creditable operational plans, supplier comparisons, and promotional copy on demand. The residual competence is judgment: deciding which AI-generated procurement or staffing recommendation actually fits a specific operation and its guests. With no licensure or accreditation lock in this hospitality program and only partial embodied-service protection, little caps the erosion, and the rating rises to High. The knowledge remains useful for oversight, but the routine management execution the course teaches is increasingly performed competently by AI.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently handling most routine beverage-operations planning, procurement analysis, marketing, and scheduling, with the manager's role concentrated in relationship, taste, and final judgment. The specific execution this course teaches, building the plan, selecting the inventory, drafting the marketing, is substantially automatable, and absent any institutional brake the rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty is how much of hospitality management restructures around AI versus how much the embodied, guest-facing service dimension keeps humans central; the partial protection from hands-on service appraisal is real but does not reach the deterministic threshold to lower the band. I commit to High while acknowledging the hospitality labor market may reorganize rather than simply shrink, which is an enrollment question outside this instrumental rating.
BVG 2015.d: Students in this course examine the importance of responsible beverage service in hospitality settings. Practical hands on experience focuses on how to manage the beverage option of a restaurant, hotel, bar, or event. Students investigate the requirements to equip, staff, manage, and market beverage operations. Classroom activities allow for student appraisal and evaluation of the preparation and service of beverages. Course assignments and activities provide a review of the major commercially available beverages of the world to build student awareness of the procurement and selection of quality beverages for sustainable hospitality operations.

r: The applied work is introductory social-and-behavioral-science analysis: describing and explaining how culture, institutions, policy, and power shape beverage production, service, and meaning across global cases from water and tea to beer, wine, and wellness drinks, communicated responsibly. This maps to O*NET activities for getting and interpreting information and communicating meaning. The written analysis is exposed to AI, but the interpretive, critical-thinking core is what task-exposure research associates negatively with exposure, and the course adds embodied tasting and service activities. The binding constraint is institutional: this course carries a GT-Pathways Social and Behavioral Sciences and Global Diversity designation, a statutory general-education transfer mandate that keeps it in the core. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact; AI can draft cultural analysis, but the course develops the student's own analytic and communicative literacy, and the transfer designation caps erosion, holding the rating at Low.

By 2031, models will fluently produce global-beverage cultural analysis, comparative case writing, and the descriptive synthesis the course assigns, weakening the rationale for students to generate it themselves. Observed-usage data already shows writing and office tasks as a prominent category, and this course's paper-and-analysis work sits squarely there. The instrumental case shifts toward the student's own interpretive judgment and toward critically evaluating AI-generated cultural claims for plausibility and bias. The GT-Pathways general-education mandate caps the erosion by keeping the course fixed in the statewide transfer core across a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium rather than High: the analytical artifacts are increasingly automatable, but the transfer lock and the low-exposure critical-reasoning core, reinforced by tasting and service components, keep the course instrumentally necessary.

A decade out, AI will produce sophisticated cross-cultural beverage analysis on demand, and the write-it-yourself rationale is substantially eroded. But the GT-Pathways Social and Behavioral Sciences designation persists in the central case absent statewide policy change, holding the course in the general-education core, and cultivated skill in evaluating cultural and political claims retains value AI does not supply to the learner. The rating holds Medium, capped from High by the transfer mandate and from Low by the fact that much of the descriptive work automates. The honest uncertainty is pedagogical, how a globally focused appreciation-and-analysis course is taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI, not whether the general-education requirement and its critical-literacy aim remain, which in the central case they do.
BVG 2250.d: Students describe and explain how culture, institutions, policy, and power shape beverage production, service, and meaning outside the United States. Using introductory Social and Behavioral Science approaches, students examine global interconnections across cases such as water, tea/coffee, beer/wine/spirits, and non- alcoholic/wellness beverages. Emphasis is on clear description, introductory analysis, and responsible communication.In this course, students analyze the connection between global beverage styles and service to their representative culture, and their impact upon individual and societal traditions. Students enhance their awareness of global beverage culture through taste and evaluation of beverage styles, tools of service, religious, and social traditions. Students further investigate the complex human, social, political, religious, economic, and geographic influences on beverage culture. In addition to service activities, students investigate the relationship of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages to health and safety, and the importance of responsible beverage service.

r: The applied work is the safe operation of brewery equipment: understanding design and operating principles, performing basic troubleshooting and servicing of physical machinery, selecting equipment by type and style, and ultimately brewing on a pilot brewing system. These map to O*NET activities for repairing and maintaining mechanical equipment, controlling machines, and inspecting materials, categories task-exposure research places among the least automatable because they are manual and physical. A model can generate an equipment-specification list or a maintenance schedule, but it cannot diagnose a leaking valve, clean a heat exchanger, or run a pilot batch. Verification burden is high and safety-relevant: pressure, heat, and mechanical failure modes are not obvious until they manifest physically. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on brewery mechanical competence is fully intact; embodiment does the protective work in the absence of any institutional mandate.

By 2031, AI will more capably support equipment selection, generate maintenance documentation, and simulate process design, and capability trends suggest steady gains in these analytical tasks. But the course's core, physically operating, servicing, and troubleshooting real brewing equipment and running a pilot system, is not something a language or reasoning model performs. The jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant: a plausible but wrong troubleshooting suggestion applied to pressurized, hot, or electrically live equipment is dangerous, so a human who understands the machinery must verify and act. Diffusion of automation into hands-on equipment training is slow. Across a catalog cycle the pilot-brewing and servicing requirements hold. The rating stays Low; AI augments the planning and documentation, not the embodied mechanical work the course is built to teach.

Over a decade, more brewery processes will be sensor-instrumented and partly automated in commercial plants, and AI diagnostics will improve. Yet the specific competence this course builds, a student personally learning to design, select, service, and safely operate brewing equipment through a hands-on pilot project, remains embodied and is not delegable to AI on the learner's behalf. The most plausible ten-year change is that automated monitoring absorbs more routine surveillance around a still-human troubleshooting and maintenance core, not that the hands-on competence becomes unnecessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and by verification demands with real physical-safety stakes; the wider uncertainty concerns how much of brewery operation instruments itself, not whether students still need to learn to run the equipment.
BVG 2350.d: In this course, students identify the fundamental aspects of safe operation of a brewery. Activities include the basic principles for design and operation of equipment. Students perform basic troubleshooting and services to equipment. A cumulative course project results in student identification and selection of equipment and process of a brewery by type and style. At course completion, students implement their brewery design by brewing their beer on a pilot brewing system.

r: The applied work centers on the sensory taste experience: mapping the aromatic, flavor, and mouthfeel aspects of beer to style and service method, relating malting, brewing, fermentation, and aging processes to historical and modern styles, and applying that palate to beer-and-food pairing. The course description makes sensory practice explicitly critical. This maps to O*NET activities for identifying objects and events and inspecting materials through direct human perception, which task-exposure research places outside AI's automatable range because it is embodied and perceptual. A model can recite style guidelines or generate pairing suggestions, but it cannot taste, and cannot develop a student's discriminating palate. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire trained sensory competence in beer is not eroded; the informational scaffolding is exposed, but the tasting core the course is organized around is not.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate beer-style descriptions, historical context, and food-pairing recommendations, and observed-usage data shows this kind of writing is a common category, so the descriptive shell of the course grows more automatable. But the graded competence, a human learning to detect and name flavor and aroma compounds and to connect them to process and service, is not performed by any model. Verification matters because a mistaken sensory judgment misdirects style identification and pairing, a non-obvious failure best caught by a trained taster. Diffusion of automation into embodied tasting instruction lags capability. Across a catalog cycle the sensory-practice requirement holds. The rating stays Low; the knowledge component is increasingly AI-deliverable, but the perceptual, in-person skill remains the instrumental core and cannot be acquired secondhand.

A decade out, instrumented flavor analysis and AI style databases will be stronger, and more descriptive and comparative work will migrate to models. Even so, the specific competence Beers of the World builds, a personally cultivated palate that discriminates beer character and maps it to style, process, and service, is embodied and not a task AI executes for the student. The plausible ten-year shift is that AI handles more of the factual and comparative content around a still-human tasting core, not that sensory competence becomes unnecessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by the perceptual, in-person nature of the skill that task-exposure research consistently places among the least exposed. The uncertainty concerns how much analytical content automates, not whether a student pursuing beer expertise still needs to learn to taste.
BVG 3010.d: Students in this course investigate the malting, brewing, fermentation, and aging processes as they are related to historical and modern beer styles. Students apply an awareness of beer styles to the principles of beer and food pairing. Critical to the course is student practice of the sensory taste experience to map the aspects of beer and how the taste experience relates to beer style and the method served. Students compare the interpretation of historical beer styles to the current United States craft brewing industry.

r: The applied work is brewery-business planning and operations: constructing a startup business plan, translating it into the design of brewing and retail spaces under world-class manufacturing principles, and formulating plans for legal requirements, equipment, supplies, maintenance, and safety. These map to O*NET activities for developing strategies, planning and prioritizing work, and analyzing data, the business-planning tasks observed-usage data shows as a prominent AI-use category and that task-exposure research associates positively with exposure. The course also requires producing a beer, an embodied element that is somewhat protective. But the dominant deliverable is the plan and operational design, which AI drafts creditably. At 24 months adoption remains uneven and the human still owns final judgment on space design and process, so the instrumental need is partly but not wholly eroded; the rating sits at Medium.

By 2031, AI will draft business plans, financial projections, facility layouts, and compliance and maintenance schedules with facility, and enterprise deployments already automate the majority of this back-office planning work. The rationale for a student to learn to produce a brewery business plan and operational design themselves erodes materially, shifting toward specifying intent and judging whether an AI-generated plan is sound for a particular site and market. With no licensure or accreditation lock in this hospitality program and only partial protection from the physical beer-production component, little caps the erosion, and the rating rises to High. The connection between plan and physical production remains a human synthesis, but the planning execution the course teaches is increasingly performed competently by AI, matching the trajectory of comparable management and operations coursework.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently generating most brewery business planning, facility design drafts, and operational and compliance schedules, with the operator concentrated in judgment, taste, and physical execution. The specific planning-and-design execution this course teaches is substantially automatable, and absent any institutional brake the rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty is how much the hands-on production and site-specific judgment keep humans central versus how thoroughly planning automates; the partial protection from producing an actual beer is real but does not reach the deterministic threshold to lower the band. I commit to High while noting that the brewery-operator role may reorganize around AI planning rather than vanish, an enrollment consideration outside this instrumental question.
BVG 3350.d: In this course, students discuss the components of a business plan for a brewery startup. The brewery business plan is applied to the planning and design of brewing and retail spaces to assure the application of World-Class manufacturing principles. Students produce a beer to identify the relationship between the business plan and the scientific and technological requirements of quality manufacturing. Students formulate plans for managing the key aspects of brewery operations, legal requirements, equipment, supplies, maintenance, and safety of a successful brewery and retail space.

r: This one-credit variable-topics course examines global wine regions, comparing the historical and cultural events that shaped them and emphasizing grape growing and harvesting, logistics of location, climate, and cultural heritage, with tasting and sensory analysis complementing class discussion. The dominant applied work is informational: getting, analyzing, and communicating regional, historical, and geographic knowledge, which maps to O*NET activities for getting information and interpreting meaning, tasks observed-usage data shows are heavily represented in AI use and task-exposure research associates positively with exposure. The tasting component adds a somewhat protective embodied element, but the description frames it as complementing rather than anchoring the course. At 24 months adoption is still partial and the human still curates and judges, so the instrumental need is only partly eroded; the rating sits at Medium. Confidence is low given the thin one-credit description.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate the regional profiles, historical-cultural comparisons, and viticulture-and-climate explanations that constitute most of this course's content, and observed-usage data already places this descriptive writing among the most common applications. The rationale for a student to compile and analyze wine-region knowledge themselves erodes substantially. The residual protection is the sensory-analysis component, a human tasting skill AI cannot perform, but as a complement rather than the course's spine it does not, under the deterministic rule, drop the band. With no general-education designation or other institutional lock on this variable-topics offering, little caps the erosion, and the rating rises to High. The knowledge remains useful for context and judgment, but the informational execution the course centers on is increasingly automatable.

A decade out, AI will produce sophisticated, current wine-region analysis and cultural-historical synthesis on demand, and the compile-it-yourself rationale for the informational core is largely eroded. The tasting and sensory-analysis element retains genuine human value AI cannot supply, but it is a supporting activity in a knowledge-centered one-credit course, so it does not lower the rating under the rule. Absent any transfer mandate or accreditation brake, the rating holds High. The honest uncertainty is meaningful here: a fuller course description emphasizing sensory training over regional knowledge could justify a lower rating, which is why confidence is low. As described, the instrumental case rests mainly on informational work that AI increasingly performs competently, and I commit to High for the 10-year horizon on that basis.
BVG 3610.d: In this course, students examine global wine regions. Students compare and contrast major historical and cultural events that have given shape to these regions and created a strong wine culture. There is a strong emphasis on the growing and harvesting, logistics of location, as well as climate and cultural heritage of significant wine regions. Class discussion is complemented by tasting and sensory analysis of regional wines of the world.

r: The applied work is the appreciation of wine's sensory aspects: aromatics, taste, and the interaction of wine with food, together with wine service and the critical appraisal of quality, for students without prior wine knowledge. Even as it introduces grape varieties, styles, growing, and winemaking, the graded competence centers on the human perceptual act of tasting and evaluating, plus the embodied practice of service. These map to O*NET activities for identifying objects and events through perception and working directly with the public, categories task-exposure research places outside AI's automatable range. A model can explain varietals or generate tasting notes, but it cannot smell, taste, or pour. At 24 months the instrumental need to cultivate a discriminating palate and service competence is not eroded; the informational content is exposed, but the sensory and service core is embodied.

By 2031, AI will fluently produce varietal explanations, tasting-note templates, and pairing guidance, offloading the descriptive and preparatory work, consistent with observed usage skewing toward augmentation rather than substitution in these knowledge tasks. But whether a student still needs to develop their own palate and wine-service technique is unchanged: no model performs the perceptual discrimination or the real-time service the course grades. Verification burden is meaningful because appraising wine quality and diagnosing faults is a judgment a trained human makes and checks. Across a catalog cycle the sensory-and-service requirement holds. The rating stays Low; the tools reshape how tasting notes and background knowledge are produced, not the embodied appreciation and service competence Wine Fundamentals is built to develop in novices.

A decade out, instrumented aroma-and-flavor analysis and AI wine databases will be stronger, and more descriptive and educational content will migrate to models. The plausible ten-year change is that AI supplies more background and note-taking around a still-human tasting-and-service core, not that sensory appreciation becomes unnecessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by the perceptual and interpersonal nature of the skill that task-exposure research places among the least exposed. The uncertainty concerns how much informational content automates, not whether learning to taste and serve wine still requires doing it.
BVG 3613.d: Students in this course engage in the appreciation of the sensory aspects of wine, including aromatics, taste, and the interaction of wine with food. The course is intended for students without prior wine knowledge in order to gain appreciation for how wine contributes to formal and informal gatherings and celebrations around the world. Major topics include an introduction to grape varieties, wine styles, the growing of grapes, the wine making process, wine service, and critical appraisal of wine quality.

r: The applied work is hands-on exploration of brewing beer and distilling spirits in commercial facilities: observing and engaging the entire production process through malting, brewing, fermenting, finishing, conditioning, and packaging, plus the stages of spirit distillation and aging, and conducting sensory analysis of global beer and spirit styles to judge quality. These map to O*NET activities for controlling machines and processes, monitoring materials, and identifying events through perception, all placed by task-exposure research among the least automatable because they are physical and sensory. A model can narrate the production sequence or describe a style, but it cannot run a still, monitor a mash, or taste a spirit. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on production familiarity and trained sensory judgment is fully intact; the descriptive knowledge is exposed, the embodied practice is not.

By 2031, AI will more capably explain production processes, generate style descriptions, and support documentation, and capability continues to advance quickly, but adoption into hands-on production-and-tasting instruction lags. The course's core, physically observing and engaging commercial brewing and distilling and personally evaluating beer and spirit styles, is not performed by any model. Verification burden is real in a facility with pressurized, hot, and flammable processes, where a plausible but wrong judgment carries physical risk and non-obvious failure. Across a catalog cycle the facility-based and sensory requirements hold. The rating stays Low; AI augments the explanatory and comparative content, not the embodied production exposure and perceptual competence the course is organized to deliver in commercial settings.

A decade out, more brewing and distilling steps will be instrumented and partly automated in commercial plants, and AI will handle more of the descriptive and analytical content. Even so, the specific competence this course builds, a student personally experiencing the production process and developing sensory discrimination across global beer and spirit styles, is embodied and not delegable to AI on the learner's behalf. The plausible ten-year shift is that automation absorbs more routine monitoring around a still-human production-and-tasting core, not that the hands-on and perceptual competence becomes unnecessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment, verification demands, and the perceptual nature of sensory evaluation that task-exposure research consistently places outside AI's reach. The uncertainty is how much of production instruments itself, not whether students still learn by doing and tasting.
BVG 3683.d: In this course, students observe hands-on exploration of brewing beer and distilling spirits in commercial facilities. Course concepts are grounded in the cultural and historical context of these beverages. Students delve into the sensory, scientific, and technical aspects of the entire production process, including malting, brewing, fermenting, finishing, conditioning, and packaging of beer. The course then extends to the principles of spirit distillation, covering the key stages of distillation and aging. Through sensory analysis of global beer and spirit styles, students will develop an understanding of quality standards and appreciation for their role in hospitality settings and social contexts.

r: The applied work moves from knowledge of fermentation and distillation stages and spirit styles into two embodied competencies: sensory evaluation, mapping how ingredients, production, and aging shape a spirit's taste, and the practice of mixology and cocktail service, including the tools, techniques, and means of delivering a quality guest experience. These map to O*NET activities for performing physical activities, handling objects, working directly with the public, and identifying events through perception, categories task-exposure research places firmly outside AI's automatable range. A model can generate a cocktail recipe or a tasting note, but it cannot build a drink, judge balance by taste, or serve a guest in real time. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire mixology, service, and sensory competence is not eroded; the informational scaffolding is exposed, the psychomotor and interpersonal core is not.

Whether a mixology student still needs to develop hands-on cocktail technique, sensory judgment, and live service is unchanged: no model performs the psychomotor act or reads and responds to a guest. Verification burden persists because a mis-poured or mis-balanced drink, or a mistaken quality judgment, is caught by a trained human. Across a catalog cycle the practice-based service and tasting requirements hold. A decade out, AI will design cocktails and generate service scripts effortlessly, and automated dispensing exists in some settings. The plausible ten-year change is in how menus and recipes are generated and how automation handles some volume dispensing, not in whether learning to make and serve cocktails requires doing it. The rating holds Low, anchored by the psychomotor, perceptual, and interpersonal nature of the work that task-exposure research places among the least exposed. The uncertainty concerns the surrounding bar-labor market, not the instrumental necessity of acquiring the hands-on craft.
BVG 3685.d: Students in this course investigate the primary fermentation and distillation stages for the production of a variety of spirit styles. The process of spirit production is introduced relevant to the historical and modern production techniques, and recognized styles. Students apply their awareness of spirit styles to the sensory evaluation of spirits to map how the aspects of the spirit ingredients, production, and aging effect the quality of the taste experience. With an improved awareness of spirit styles, students practice the mixology and service of spirit cocktails. Service practice includes the tools, techniques, and means of service for a quality guest experience.

r: The applied work is regulatory and legal-compliance knowledge: navigating brewery licensing, alcohol distribution laws, city zoning, real estate contracts, and proper labeling and selling of beer, spirits, and wine, plus forming a corporation and achieving compliance to sell through tasting rooms and off-premises accounts, focused on Colorado but covering all fifty states. These map to O*NET activities for evaluating information against standards, analyzing information, and documenting compliance, fully digital knowledge work with no embodiment. Task-exposure research ranks tax preparers and similar rule-application work among the most exposed occupations, so the base automatability is high. But verification burden tempers it: a wrong licensing or labeling conclusion is costly and adversarial, checked by regulators. By 2031, AI will competently retrieve statutes, compare state alcohol regimes, draft entity-formation and licensing checklists, and flag labeling requirements, and observed usage already shows this legal-and-office drafting as a common category. The distinctive residue is verification: models fabricate plausible but wrong legal citations, the jagged-frontier failure mode, and in a licensing context that error is expensive, so a human who understands the law must check the output. But with no licensure lock on this course itself and no embodiment, that verification value does not cap the band, and the rating rises to High. The compliance-knowledge execution the course teaches is increasingly performed, if not fully trusted, by AI.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently handling most alcohol-beverage regulatory research, entity-formation drafting, and compliance-checklist work across states, with the human role concentrated in judgment and accountability for correctness. The rule-application execution this course teaches is substantially automatable, and absent any institutional brake the rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty is how much the persistent fabrication-and-liability problem keeps trained humans in the loop as verifiers versus how far trusted legal-AI tooling advances; that verification need raises the value of the knowledge but, under the deterministic rule, does not lower the exposure band here. I commit to High while noting that compliance work is likely to reorganize around AI drafting under human sign-off rather than disappear, a labor-structure point outside this instrumental rating.
BVG 3750.d: In this course students are introduced to the concepts and information regarding legally creating and selling alcohol in Colorado and the United States. Students will delve into the complex and ever-changing world of brewery licensing, alcohol distribution laws, city zoning, real estate contracts and proper labeling and selling of beer, spirits and wine. Furthermore, students will learn the basics of creating a corporation or company and becoming legally compliant to sell beer through both a tasting room and through off-premises accounts such as liquor stores and restaurants. This class will focus on Colorado laws, however, all 50 states will be covered so students are prepared to work around the country. Upon completion, students will be able to feel confident in avoiding pitfalls and errors commonly seen with startup breweries.

r: The applied work is sensory quality analysis: illustrating the biological and chemical principles behind beer's aromatic and taste expressions, practicing hedonic and analytical sensory evaluation procedures, and troubleshooting trace beer faults back to their source in the brewing process. These map to O*NET activities for identifying objects and events through perception, inspecting materials, and evaluating against standards, work that is both perceptual and grounded in scientific reasoning, categories task-exposure research places among the least exposed. By 2031, instrumented analysis and AI will more capably identify some chemical fault markers and explain their origins, and models will draft the theoretical content fluently. Verification burden is central: a mistaken fault diagnosis misdirects a brewery's corrective action, a costly and non-obvious failure best caught by a trained taster who understands the underlying chemistry. Across a catalog cycle the sensory-evaluation and fault-tracing requirements hold. The rating stays Low; AI supports the analytical chemistry and documentation, not the embodied hedonic and analytical evaluation the course is built to train, which remains the instrumental core.

A decade out, analytical instrumentation and AI pattern-matching will catch more fault compounds automatically, and the balance of the course could shift toward interpreting instrument output. But the human competence this course builds, perceiving, naming, and tracing beer faults to their process source through trained sensory judgment, remains embodied and reasoning-intensive, precisely what task-exposure research finds resistant. The plausible ten-year change is that instruments handle more routine detection around a still-human interpretive-and-troubleshooting core, not that sensory competence becomes unnecessary. The rating holds Low, anchored by the perceptual nature of the skill and the verification demands of quality decisions. The uncertainty is how much routine analytical detection automates, not whether a brewing-quality professional still needs a trained palate and fault-diagnosis judgment.
BVG 3810.d: In this course, students illustrate the biological and chemical principles that lead to aromatic, taste, and taste expressions in beer. Students practice procedures for hedonic and analytical sensory evaluation of beer. Students troubleshoot and process trace beer faults to their source in the brewing process.

r: The applied work connects brewing-process conditions to the flavor characteristics of each beer style and exercises in-depth sensory analysis through open and blind tastings, recognizing production and storage faults, comparing draft-system design and operation, and detailing beer-and-food pairing. r: This capstone applies product-development skill to commercial beer production: students synthesize prior coursework into a critical analysis of operational, promotional, technical, talent-management, and sensory aspects, deliver a written and oral product plan with a finished beer, direct peers in a large-batch production, and publicly propose and promote their product, integrating financial, promotional, operational, and managerial requirements. The dominant deliverables, the analysis, business-and-marketing plan, and promotional pitch, map to O*NET activities for developing strategies, analyzing information, and influencing others, which observed-usage data shows as prominent AI-use categories and task-exposure research associates positively with exposure. The embodied elements, directing a live production and presenting in person, are somewhat protective. But the graded core is planning and promotion knowledge work. At 24 months adoption is uneven and the human still integrates and leads, so the instrumental need is partly eroded; the rating sits at Medium.

By 2031, AI will draft the operational analyses, financial projections, marketing and promotional materials, and product plans that anchor this capstone, and enterprise deployments already automate the majority of such planning-and-writing work. The rationale for a student to produce the integrated plan themselves erodes materially, shifting toward specifying intent, integrating across domains, and judging whether AI-generated components cohere into a viable product. The live team-leadership and physical large-batch production remain human, partial protection, but as one component of a planning-heavy deliverable it does not reach the deterministic threshold to lower the band, and with no institutional lock in this hospitality program the rating rises to High. The capstone's synthesis-and-promotion execution is increasingly performed competently by AI, matching the trajectory of comparable integrative management coursework.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently generating most of the operational analysis, financial and marketing planning, and promotional material a beer product launch requires, with the human concentrated in leadership, taste, and final integrative judgment. The planning-and-promotion execution this capstone teaches is substantially automatable, and absent any institutional brake the rating holds High. The genuine uncertainty is how much the embodied production leadership and live public promotion keep humans central versus how thoroughly the analytical and planning work automates; that protection is real but does not, under the deterministic rule, lower the band. I commit to High while noting the capstone's terminal, integrative role and that the brewing-entrepreneur function may reorganize around AI planning rather than disappear, a labor-structure point outside this instrumental rating.
BVG 4850.d: This course is an application of both theoretical and practical product development skills in the brewing industry. Students direct their peers and are evaluated in the large batch production of a beer inclusive of the skillset gained in prior coursework to include the financial, promotional, and operational, and managerial requirements of beer production. Students publicly propose and promote their beer product to demonstrate their mastery the comprehensive aspects of planning and producing a beer for the marketplace.
